Control experiments comparing the luminescent responses of the NiMOF with varying Ag layer thicknesses will validate the effectiveness of the Ag integration, while the detection limits of 3-NT and HA will be quantitatively assessed through statistical analysis of calibration curves.

The incorporation of a nickel(II) metal-organic framework (NiMOF) functionalized with Eu(III) ions at a concentration of 0.1 mol% and simultaneously embedded with specific amine and carboxylate groups will result in a novel dual-emission ratiometric luminescent sensor. This sensor will enable selective detection of 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT) and hippuric acid (HA) in serum and urine, demonstrating enhanced sensitivity through distinct modulation of emission at 441 nm (turn-on for HA) and 628 nm (turn-off for 3-NT). The luminescence response will be operational under physiological conditions (pH 7.4, temperature 37°C) and characterized through robust calibration curves, alongside evaluations of accuracy and reproducibility utilizing both synthetic and real sample analysis. The unique binding interactions via the functional groups will optimize the sensor’s performance in practical clinical scenarios, while the implemented competitive binding assays will validate its efficacy in differentiating between these biomarkers at clinically relevant concentrations, providing significant implications for diagnostic and monitoring applications in human health.

The development of a bifunctional luminescence sensor through the strategic incorporation of both Eu(III) ions and a dansyl fluorophore into a nickel(II) metal-organic framework (NiMOF) via a meticulously controlled post-synthetic embedding and modification process will yield a high-performance dual-emission ratiometric sensor. This sensor will enable the simultaneous, selective, and ultra-sensitive detection of biomarkers 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT) and hippuric acid (HA) in serum and urine. It will exhibit optimized emission signals at 441 nm for HA (turn-on) and 628 nm for 3-NT (turn-off) under physiological conditions (pH 7.4, temperature 25°C), achieving detection limits lower than the previously reported 229 nM for Cu(II) and 539 nM for 3-NT. The sensor's performance will be validated through rigorous quantitative calibration curves, robust statistical analyses (e.g., linear regression with high r² values), and specificity testing against potential interferents, while also elucidating the binding mechanisms responsible for the emission changes.

A nickel(II) metal-organic framework (NiMOF) engineered to operate as a bifunctional luminescence sensor for the detection of 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT) and hippuric acid (HA) in serum and urine exploits a dual-mode sensing strategy. This is achieved through precise post-synthetic modification to embed fluorometric linkers that promote specific interactions with nitro groups in 3-NT and facilitate hydrogen bonding or π-π stacking with HA. Concurrently, a novel layer-by-layer assembly method calibrates a photonic crystal structure within the NiMOF to achieve a tailored photonic bandgap of 470–630 nm, enhancing luminescence signals specific to these interactions. The dual-mode system integrates optical signal amplification with distinct luminescent signatures for each biomarker, ensuring nanomolar sensitivity and selectivity. Real-world viability will be verified through a tiered validation strategy, starting with controlled conditions simulating biological matrices and advancing to real serum and urine tests. This research addresses current diagnostic limitations by advancing the sensitivity and specificity of biomarker detection and suggests broader applicability to diverse biomarker sensing applications.

A nickel(II) metal-organic framework (NiMOF) can be engineered with an integrated layered photonic crystal structure through a controlled layer-by-layer assembly technique, optimizing the photonic crystal periodicity to enhance luminescent signals specifically for 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT) and hippuric acid (HA) detection. This system utilizes non-quenching silica as the photonic material to ensure luminescence preservation and employs π-π interactions and hydrogen bonding to achieve selective biomarker recognition. By tailoring the photonic bandgap to overlap with the emission wavelengths of NiMOF-bound biomarkers (anticipated in the 450–650 nm range), this approach aims to create a bifunctional luminescence sensor with a nanomolar detection threshold for these biomarkers in both simplified solutions and complex matrices like serum and urine. Initial experiments will focus on demonstrating selectivity and sensitivity in controlled conditions before validating performance in biological samples, thus paving the way for novel diagnostic applications.

A nickel(II) metal-organic framework (NiMOF) can be engineered as a bifunctional luminescent sensor specifically for 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT) and hippuric acid (HA). This is achieved by incorporating quinone moieties into the MOF as part of its organic linker, providing enzyme-mimicking catalytic sites that facilitate selective redox reactions. This integration leads to analyte-specific luminescence shifts measurable through time-resolved photoluminescence spectroscopy. Notably, the selective integration of quinone moieties at designated sites enhances the structural stability of the NiMOF during these electrochemical transformations. Different experimental conditions, such as pH and temperature, will be optimized for each analyte to maximize sensitivity and selectivity, with predicted luminescence shifts accurately characterizing both 3-NT and HA in complex biological matrices.

A nickel(II) metal-organic framework (NiMOF) with a dual-functional design, incorporating urea-functionalized dicarboxylate ligands and quinone-enriched co-linkers, is proposed as a bifunctional luminescent sensor for the simultaneous, sensitive, and selective detection of 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT) and hippuric acid (HA) in serum and urine. The urea-functionalized ligands establish specific hydrogen bonding interactions with HA, leading to measurable luminescence enhancement, while the quinone-enriched co-linkers mimic enzymatic redox activity to facilitate selective and rapid luminescence quenching of 3-NT. The framework structure combines a three-dimensional pillared-layer motif with optimized interpenetration to enhance stability in complex physiological environments and improve analyte-specific diffusion kinetics. Computational simulations and molecular docking will be employed to refine pore size, ligand functionality, and analyte interaction, ensuring maximal sensitivity and reducing cross-reactivity. Excitation wavelength tuning and time-resolved photoluminescence spectrometry will enable robust detection mechanisms that remain resilient to interference from other biomolecules commonly found in biological matrices. Furthermore, the sensor’s reusability and stability in varying pH conditions and physiological fluids will be validated through recycling experiments and stability assays. This system is aimed at advancing clinical diagnostics by providing accurate, high-throughput detection of biomarkers critical for monitoring oxidative stress and metabolic disorders.

This bifunctional design will create a luminescent sensor capable of exhibiting enhanced sensitivity and selectivity for detecting 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT) and hippuric acid (HA) in complex biological fluids such as serum and urine. Performance will be systematically evaluated through detailed fluorescence emission spectra analysis, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and pH-dependent luminescent behavior. The optimization process will include a systematic exploration of ligand ratios (1:1, 1:2, and 1:3) and an evaluation of specific nickel coordination sites (e.g., surface vs. internal metal ions), alongside control experiments with relevant interfering compounds. The integration of complementary functionalities will be hypothesized to yield synergistic luminescent enhancements, validated by distinct shifts in emission peaks and increased quenching efficiencies when exposing the sensor to 3-NT and HA compared to controls.

The incorporation of functionalized ligands, specifically thiol- and amine-based ligands, into the nickel(II) metal-organic framework (NiMOF) will significantly enhance its luminescent properties, leading to improved sensitivity and selectivity for detecting biomarkers 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT) and hippuric acid (HA) in serum and urine samples. The optimization of ligand loading ratios and synthesis conditions will be systematically evaluated, utilizing fluorescence spectroscopy to measure luminescent responses across clinically relevant concentration ranges.

The engineered nickel(II) metal-organic framework (NiMOF), utilizing a dual-ligand system composed of urea-functionalized dicarboxylate ligands and electron-rich aromatic ligands, synthesized at an optimal temperature of 120°C for 24 hours in specific molar ratios (0.1 M for the dicarboxylate ligand and 0.05 M for the aromatic ligand), will exhibit enhanced multiresponsive luminescent detection capabilities for the simultaneous quantification of 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT) and hippuric acid (HA) in serum and urine matrices. This NiMOF is anticipated to show distinct luminescent responses influenced by π-π stacking interactions and hydrogen bonding with the target biomarkers, backed by a significant shift in emission peaks and improved luminescent quenching efficiency. The efficacy of the biosensor will be rigorously evaluated through time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy, achieving limits of detection (LOD) for both biomarkers under 50 nM and demonstrating strong anti-interference performance against common biological components using control studies.
